newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - May 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - May 22.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- BLOW FOR BIOTECH INDUSTRY

Poor trial results of its septic shock treatment have led UK pharmaceutical group Celltech to drop the drug, serving a further blow to the UK biotechnology industry. Peter Fellner, Celltech's chief executive, described the announcement as 'disappointing and unexpected'. In a further setback, industry insiders believe the announcement may prove hazardous to the biotechnology industry, as it will make investors less likely to put money into the sector.
-- GOVERNOR THOUGHT OF QUITTING OVER BANK PROPOSALS

In an indication of possible tension between Bank of England governor Eddie George and chancellor Gordon Brown, George disclosed that he had considered quitting over proposed slimming measures at the bank. Senior government members now claim George may not be reappointed for a second five-year term next year, indicating that Gavyn Davis, chief economist at US investment bank Goldman Sachs, is now the front runner for the position.
-- PILKINGTON CHIEF LEVERTON OUSTED IN BOARDROOM COUP

It has been revealed that Roger Leverton, now former chief of UK-based glass company Pilkington was ousted from his position on Wednesday in what was called a 'boardroom coup' organized by company chairman Sir Nigel Rudd. Rudd and other non-executive directors had reached an agreement that the 155 million stg restructuring of the company was proceeding too slowly, after three profit warnings, and determined that a reshuffle at the top of the company would be required for a 'change of pace'.
-- RAILTRACK CONTROLS TIGHTENED AFTER INVESTMENT CRITICISM

UK rail regulator John Swift has lashed out against Railtrack's announcement that it would invest 1 billion stg per year into track and station improvements. Swift criticized the fact that there was no way to check whether the actual investments were being spent in the 'public interest' and has made plans to hold a meeting with deputy prime minister and transport secretary John Prescott to discuss regulation of the rail industry. Swift has also planned a meeting with Railtrack officials, to discuss modifications of its licence to operate.
-- CHEAPER POWER SCHEME FOR UNION MEMBERS

Trade union members are set to receive lower gas and electricity costs, following a Trades Union Congress decision to launch a marketing subsidiary and make partnerships with supply companies, taking advantage of the liberalisation of the market in April 1998. Union Energy Ltd., the new body, is in talks with 17 energy companies hoping to receive tenders with at least three by June, which would result in cuts of up to 20 per cent in members' gas bills and up to 10 per cent in electricity bills. Of the 23 million households in the UK, and estimated 4.6 million are Union members.
-- RECORD SALES TAKE THE SPICE OUT OF LIFE

Only a week after it was revealed that the UK's Spice Girls reached the top of the US music charts, new music industry data from the British Phonographic Industry reveals that total music sales fell four per cent in the first quarter to 215.2 million stg. The album market, long detailed as the most popular area, experienced its first quarterly decline since 1996, and the while the total number of singles sold went up seven per cent, overall sales also fell as the total market shrank by 11.5 per cent in value. The BPI added that there is no indication that sales will improve in the second quarter.
-- GROUND LAID FOR AUCTION OF RADIO SPECTRUM

The UK government has unveiled further information into the planned $1.5 billion privatisation of the radio spectrum. A bill released Wednesday detailed a more efficient manner of managing the auction, with licence fees relating to the actual value of the spectrum rather than the cost of managing it which is currently 43 million stg per year. Charges will also be determined by the location of the user, with those in congested areas facing a rise in charges and those in lower populated areas seeing a possible reduction in bills.
-- CARLTON BULLISH ABOUT DIGITAL TV

Media group Carlton Communications has reported a 13 per cent increase in pre-tax profits for the six months to the end of March, to 158.6 million stg. The results, towards the top end of market expectations, also saw turnover rise 6 per cent to 896 million stg, and operating profit increase 13 per cent to 159 million stg. Announcing the results, Michael Green, Carlton chairman, forecast that digital television would mean more business for the company whatever form it took.
-- ALIZYME BUYS DRUG RIGHTS

Biotechnology company Alizyme has announced the purchase of exclusive rights for the medicinal use of a product derived from rice believed to inhibit fat digestion. Alizyme, which specialises in drugs for obesity, will conduct trials to evaluate the therapeutic potential of the product, which has been tested on a small scale by developer Yakurigakru Chou Kenkyusho.
-- COMPETITION STRIKES AT NATIONAL POWER

Energy generator National Power has reported an 8 per cent fall in annual profits before exceptionals, to 740 million stg. The news disappointed the market, which had been expecting profits of about 786 million stg. Shares in the group fell 17p to 545.5p. The company blamed 'increasingly competitive' conditions in the UK market, where wholesale electricity prices are now 4 per cent lower than a year ago.
